An enterprise system-development engagement typically progresses through several standard requirements and analysis phases before physical system design begins. These phases are designed to establish the strategic "why," define operational and governance rules, gather precise functional needs, and validate data and user expectations before engineering hours are spent. 

Based on your enterprise data management and software development sources, the standard pre-design phases, their activities, and the specific artifacts they produce include:

### 1. Data Strategy & Strategic Alignment Phase
This initial phase answers the core question: **"Why are we investing in this data or system initiative?"** [1] The primary focus is to assess the organization's current state (including existing architecture, data quality, and pain points), define strategic objectives, and align the technical project with overall business objectives and OKRs [1, 2].
*   **Typical Artifacts Produced:**
    *   **Data Strategy Roadmap / Modernization Plan:** A structured roadmap detailing prioritized initiatives, implementation timelines, and resource allocations [1-3].
    *   **AI and Analytics Strategy:** A strategic document outlining how advanced analytics, machine learning, and business intelligence capabilities will be utilized to drive business value [1-3].

### 2. Data Governance & Policy Definition Phase
This phase addresses the rules of engagement: **"What rules should guide data and system usage?"** [1] It establishes the standards, roles, and security policies (including regulatory compliance such as HIPAA, GDPR, or medical PII handling) to ensure data quality, security, and integrity across the entire data lifecycle [1, 3-6].
*   **Typical Artifacts Produced:**
    *   **Data Governance Framework:** A formal document defining data quality standards, stewardship responsibilities, compliance processes, and audit controls [1, 7, 8].
    *   **Data Ownership & Stewardship Model:** An organizational model assigning clear accountability, identifying data owners, and establishing data stewards to oversee data quality across business units [1, 2, 7, 9].
    *   **Data Policies & Business Glossary:** Standardized naming conventions, metadata specifications, and master data definitions to maintain data consistency across systems [1, 7, 8, 10].

### 3. Requirements Discovery & Specification Phase
In this phase, project managers, product managers, and business analysts meet with stakeholders across impacted business units to outline exactly **what** the team should build, its constraints, and how success will be measured [11-13]. This captures both the business drivers and the functional scope of the proposed system [13, 14].
*   **Typical Artifacts Produced:**
    *   **Business Requirements Document (BRD):** A comprehensive document detailing the project description, scope, business drivers, "as-is" vs. "proposed" processes, cost-benefit analyses, assumptions, and functional/non-functional requirements ranked by a priority rating system (Critical, High, Medium, Low, Future) [14-16].
    *   **Product Requirements Document (PRD):** A collaborative document detailing the problem statement, target user personas, user research insights, feature descriptions, non-functional constraints (such as security and performance), acceptance criteria, success metrics, and release/rollout notes [13, 17-19].
    *   **System Requirements Document:** A consolidated, structured requirements baseline that serves as the direct input to build the technical system design specifications [20].

### 4. End-User Validation & Visual Prototyping Phase
Before physical system design begins, requirements must be validated directly with stakeholders and end-users [11, 21, 22]. Reconciling conflicting stakeholder needs and identifying undocumented assumptions at this stage prevents costly rework during or after development [11, 21].
*   **Typical Artifacts Produced:**
    *   **Visual Prototypes, Workflows, & Diagrams:** Workflows, graphs, charts, diagrams, and interactive mockups used to visually articulate technical requirements to non-technical stakeholders [11].
    *   **Validated Sample Data:** A representative sample of the system's expected output (such as a sample SQL view, CSV, or dashboard mockup) provided to end-users to check business logic, data distribution, and expected usage patterns [22, 23].
    *   **Formal Stakeholder Sign-Off:** Recorded confirmation and approval from key stakeholders on requirements and acceptance criteria, establishing a baseline before database transformation or physical design begins [22, 24].

### 5. Target Data Architecture Phase
This final pre-design phase answers: **"How should enterprise data be structured?"** [25] It defines the physical and logical architectures for integrating, collecting, storing, and securing data, bridging the gap between raw business requirements and physical system development [3, 26].
*   **Typical Artifacts Produced:**
    *   **Data Architecture Blueprint:** High-level system blueprints detailing logical data models, data platforms (such as warehouses or lakes), and integration approaches [1, 2, 8, 26].
    *   **Technology Stack Definition:** An inventory of the designated storage platforms, integration pipelines, processing engines, and programming languages to be used [1, 8].

A common source of confusion in enterprise data initiatives is the distinction between enterprise data management and master data management (MDM) . Enterprise data management covers the full lifecycle of all data assets, including governance, integration, storage, and usage. MDM, on the other hand, focuses on a narrower yet critical domain to ensure a single and consistent view of key business entities such as customers, products, and suppliers. This distinction becomes especially important at scale, where master data management ensures consistency across systems. As organizations grow, inconsistencies in master data can lead to fragmented customer views, reporting discrepancies, and inefficiencies across business functions. By establishing MDM as part of the governance layer, companies can create a reliable foundation for analytics, operational processes, and cross-functional collaboration. In this context, master data management is not a standalone initiative but an essential component that strengthens the overall effectiveness of enterprise data management.

Best Practices for Documenting Business Requirements As you work your way through the template, here are eight best-practices that will guide you in documenting the business requirements and set your development project up for success: Assign resources to write the business requirements who understand all stakeholder needs and the project's software development language. Meet with stakeholders from every business unit impacted by the project—preferably in one-on-one meetings to ensure everyone is heard. Reconcile conflicts among stakeholders who disagree on a requirement; it's critical to do so before development begins. Identify the target audience for each requirement, which will factor into the end-user testing process. Ensure each requirement is testable so that achieving it can be validated. Facilitate testing by defining each requirement separately; combining two or more into one definition may make validation impossible. Specify the exact success metrics for satisfying each requirement; “easy to use” is ambiguous and difficult to define as to when it's achieved. Leverage images, graphs, charts, diagrams, workflows, use-cases and visual prototypes to articulate the documented requirements to non-technical stakeholders.

The Product Requirements Document (PRD): Definition and Purpose What defines a PRD? A PRD is the working document product managers use to describe what a team should build and why it matters. It provides engineering and design with clarity on (1) scope, (2) constraints, (3) acceptance criteria, and (4) expected customer value . The goal is alignment. A well-written product requirements document outlines the problem to solve, the intended outcome, and the key requirements needed to deliver that outcome. When it is clear and current, it reduces rework and supports faster decision making across technical teams.

Enterprise Data Management Architecture A data management architecture is your organization's blueprint for collecting, storing, securing, arranging, integrating, and using data through interconnected management systems. There's no one-size-fits-all architecture; it's shaped by business needs, goals, and constraints. Common approaches to enterprise data management architecture are: Monolithic architecture . All data is handled by a single centralized data store. It's simple in implementation but comes with high latency and limited scalability. Distributed data mesh . Domain-specific data owners handle their data products and pipelines, with the architecture consisting of smaller decentralized components. It offers better scalability and flexibility, but is more complex in implementation.
